title: Your mother's eyes
hook: We returned you to your mother so her eyes might be cooled (20:40)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Umar hears Ta-Ha, and your line was the page changed him. Did you reread something that once changed you? What did it say this time? Day four hundred seventy-seven.

Musa is standing in a sacred valley, barefoot, having just been told he's a prophet and sent to Pharaoh. He asks for help: his brother Harun beside him, a tongue that speaks more easily. And God, before sending him, does something tender. He reminds Musa of his own story, from before Musa could remember anything. A baby, a box, a river. And a mother on the riverbank, watching it float away.

Pharaoh was killing the baby boys of the Children of Israel. Ta-Ha says God inspired Musa's mother: put him in a chest, and put the chest in the river. The river will throw it onto the bank, and an enemy of Mine and his will take him. Consider the instruction. To save your child, let him go, toward the very palace that wants him dead. Another surah, Al-Qasas, says her heart was left empty, and she nearly gave the secret away. Then, verse thirty-nine: I cast love on you from Me, so you'd be raised under My eye. The baby is taken into Pharaoh's house and loved there. But he won't nurse from any woman they bring. And his sister, who has been following the chest along the bank, steps forward and says, in Pickthall's words, "Shall I show you one who will nurse him?" And then, verse forty: "and We restored thee to thy mother that her eyes might be refreshed and might not sorrow." In Arabic, kay taqarra 'aynuha: so that her eye might be cooled. Coolness of the eye is an old Arabic way of saying deep joy and relief. One explanation in the classical dictionaries: tears of grief are hot, and tears of joy are cool. The Qur'an uses the phrase elsewhere too: a prayer for spouses and children who are a coolness of the eyes. So God, sending Musa to face Pharaoh, reminds him of this: you were saved, and you were brought back, and the reason given is a mother's grief. Before the miracles and the staff and the sea, there was a woman by a river, and God did not leave her crying.
screen: `A CHEST ON THE RIVER.` · `HER HEART LEFT EMPTY.` · `A SISTER ON THE BANK.` · `COOL EYES: THE TEARS OF JOY.` · then, large: `THAT HER EYES MIGHT BE REFRESHED.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a mother: your own, a grandmother, a friend who's just had a baby, a woman who mothered you though she wasn't your mother, or one who's grieving a child. Picture her face. What is she carrying right now that you could lighten, even a little? A call. A visit. A meal. Telling her one thing she did right. If she's died, you can do something kind in her name. If you pray, you can pray for her. The bell holds the time.
Musa. Returned to his mother as a baby so that her eyes might be cooled, and she would not grieve. Today's word.
Your line: so she would not grieve. Today, bring one small comfort to a mother: a call, a kind word, a help with something heavy. Day four hundred seventy-seven.

howItsDone: Muslims retell the story of Musa's mother as a lesson in trust and in God's care for mothers; the phrase qurrat 'ayn, coolness of the eye, is common in Muslim speech and in the du'a of 25:74 for spouses and children.

fork.reveal: she offers a nurse, and Musa is returned to his own mother, so her eyes might be cooled and she would not grieve (20:40).

original.note: Arabic: so that her eye might be cooled (20:40), the idiom for deep joy.

trapdoor: what you thought: baby Musa was saved from Pharaoh.
what it means: God gives Musa back to his mother, and the reason the verse names is her grief.
what a scholar hears: qurrat al-'ayn is explained by some lexicographers as cool tears of joy against hot tears of grief; Ta-Ha frames the story as a reminder at Tuwa.
recall: the green one; named in hadith

notes: Pickthall wording of 20:40 quoted from memory (both the sister's question and the clause about the mother's eyes); confirm exactly.
The lexicographers' explanation of qurrat 'ayn (cool tears of joy, hot tears of grief) is a classical explanation among several; confirm.
The detail that Musa refused the wet nurses is from 28:12; the script attributes 'her heart was left empty' to Al-Qasas (28:10).
Editor review (2026-10-01): cut 'He's frightened' (not in 20:9–36); the hot/cold tears explanation is now one classical explanation, not the lexicographers' consensus.
